matrix.source_timing_explanation: Weekly or more often, based on sensitivity
review_questions: Compare in-scope assets with automated backup coverage and schedules. Confirm backups run at least weekly, with greater frequency when data sensitivity requires it.
Inspect recent job results for successful execution and missing, failed or incomplete jobs. A weekly evidence review is not a substitute for weekly backup execution.
evidence_examples: Backup scope and schedule configuration together with dated job results.
Client or provider backup reports showing success, failure and subsequent resolution.

requirement_guide.plain: Run automated backups at least weekly, or more often when the data's sensitivity calls for it. Backups need to execute successfully; reviewing a weekly report is not the same as making a weekly backup.
requirement_guide.start: Compare the asset and recovery scope with automated backup coverage. Ask IT to show recent scheduled jobs and their actual results. Follow missing or failed jobs to see whether a usable backup was subsequently created.
requirement_guide.evidence: Scope and schedule settings explain what should run. Dated job results establish execution, including failures. A provider report can support this if it identifies the relevant systems and outcomes, not just that backup service is included in a contract.
requirement_guide.ask: What is backed up automatically at least weekly? Does sensitivity require more frequent backups for some data? Which jobs failed or were missed? What result confirms the backup eventually completed?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate schedules with no successful jobs, newly added systems outside backup coverage, or failures hidden inside a green summary. A plan to rerun a failed job does not mean a backup already exists.

matrix.title: Protect Recovery Data
matrix.authored_summary: Protect backups consistently with original-data sensitivity.
review_questions: Compare recovery-data protections with those required for the original data.

Inspect access and other relevant controls, including encryption or separation where the data requirements call for them. A protected destination alone does not establish the separate isolation requirement in 11.4.
evidence_examples: Backup access/encryption configurations compared with the original data's protection requirements.
Provider protection records or demonstrations covering the recovery copy.

requirement_guide.plain: Protect recovery copies as carefully as the original information. A backup can contain the same sensitive records, so it should not become an easier way to read or alter them. Equivalent protection depends on the original data's requirements.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the data owner what protection the original information needs. With IT, compare that with backup access and other relevant safeguards, such as encryption where required. Include the provider's recovery copies in the comparison.
requirement_guide.evidence: Original-data protection requirements provide the comparison point. Backup access settings, relevant encryption settings or provider protection records can demonstrate equivalent treatment. Isolation evidence addresses a different question under safeguard 11.4.
requirement_guide.ask: Who can read or change the backup compared with the original data? Are its required protections maintained during storage and handling? What can provider personnel access? Can you demonstrate the actual settings?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for sensitive backups in broadly accessible folders, recovery copies lacking protection applied to originals, or vague claims that a destination is secure. Backup isolation alone does not establish equivalent confidentiality protection.

matrix.title: Establish and Maintain an Isolated Instance of Recovery Data
matrix.authored_summary: Maintain a backup copy isolated from primary-system compromise.
review_questions: Identify the isolated recovery-data instance and inspect how its isolation is maintained.

Confirm it is an actual maintained recovery copy, not merely a proposed destination. Offline, cloud or off-site arrangements are examples; their location or a restricted folder alone does not demonstrate isolation.
evidence_examples: Backup destination/version configuration and records identifying the isolated copy.
Access or separation details from the client or provider showing how isolation is maintained.

requirement_guide.plain: Maintain an isolated recovery copy so a problem affecting normal systems is less likely to affect every backup too. Offline, off-site and cloud arrangements can help, but their label or location alone does not prove isolation.
requirement_guide.start: Ask IT to identify the specific isolated recovery copy that exists today. Have the team explain what separates it from normal systems and routine access. Check that the copy is maintained rather than merely planned.
requirement_guide.evidence: Destination and version records can identify the copy. Access and separation configurations can explain its isolation. Provider records may support the mechanism; a diagram of a future backup arrangement is not evidence of a maintained instance.
requirement_guide.ask: Which recovery copy is isolated? What keeps normal system activity or compromised access from affecting it? How is it maintained? If it is off site or in the cloud, what actually provides the isolation?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate a second folder on the same exposed system, a cloud copy controlled by the same unrestricted access, or an offline copy no longer updated. Multiple copies are not automatically isolated copies.

matrix.title: Ensure Network Infrastructure is Up-to-Date
matrix.authored_summary: Verify network software support and maintain current infrastructure.
review_questions: Review network device/software versions and supported service offerings to confirm infrastructure is kept current. CIS examples include latest stable software and supported network-as-a-service.
Compare versions with vendor support information monthly or more frequently. Identify unsupported or outdated infrastructure rather than treating a replacement plan as a current implementation.
evidence_examples: Network version inventory and vendor lifecycle/release information.
Dated monthly support checks and upgrade or provider maintenance results.

requirement_guide.plain: Keep network infrastructure current and supported, checking software support at least monthly. Network infrastructure includes the equipment and services connecting systems. Current stable software and supported managed network services are examples of ways to meet this expectation.
requirement_guide.start: Ask IT or the network provider for device and software versions. Compare them with vendor support and stable-release information. Identify who performs the monthly support check and how outdated infrastructure is addressed.
requirement_guide.evidence: A network version inventory paired with vendor information can establish current support. Dated monthly checks and upgrade results can show maintenance. Provider records can cover managed services without assuming the contract alone proves current versions.
requirement_guide.ask: Which network components are unsupported or behind current stable software? When was support last checked? Who handles updates for managed equipment? Can we see installed versions and completed maintenance results?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for network devices absent from inventories, firmware never checked after installation, or unsupported equipment covered only by a replacement plan. Hardware still functioning is not the same as software still supported.

matrix.title: Establish and Maintain a Security Awareness Program
matrix.authored_summary: Maintain an awareness program and review content; track workforce participation.
matrix.source_timing_explanation: Training at hire and annually; content review annually and on significant change
review_questions: Review the awareness program and workforce training records. Confirm training on secure use of assets and data takes place at hire and at least annually.
Compare participation with the workforce population to find missed hires or overdue training. Verify content is reviewed/updated annually and after significant changes affecting the program.
evidence_examples: Training content and hire/annual completion records from internal or provider-led delivery.
Workforce reconciliation and dated content reviews/revisions.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach the workforce how to use systems and information securely when hired and at least annually. Maintain the training content through annual review and significant relevant changes. Purchasing training does not establish that people received it.
requirement_guide.start: Ask HR or the awareness owner for training content and completion records. Compare them with the workforce and recent hires. Identify missed people and check when the content was last reviewed for current working practices.
requirement_guide.evidence: Course materials show what is taught. Attendance or completion records show delivery. Workforce reconciliation and content-review records can together demonstrate hire-time and annual coverage without requiring a particular training platform.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask HR or the training owner: How do new hires receive security training? Who is overdue for annual training? Are relevant workforce groups included? When was the content updated after changes to how we work?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate new starters missing training, annual lists that omit parts of the workforce, or completion records for content nobody maintains. An email announcing an available course does not establish participation.

matrix.title: Train Workforce Members to Recognize Social Engineering Attacks
matrix.authored_summary: Teach recognition of phishing and other social manipulation.
review_questions: Review training content and delivery records for recognizing social engineering, including examples such as phishing, business email compromise, pretexting and tailgating.
Confirm the topic is actually taught within the awareness program. A phishing simulation can support evaluation but is not a mandatory IG1 artifact.
evidence_examples: Relevant lesson material and training/attendance records.
Discussion, exercise or knowledge-check results where used by the organization.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach people to recognize attempts to manipulate them into unsafe actions. Examples include deceptive messages, fake payment instructions, invented identities and following someone into a restricted area. This is broader than recognizing suspicious email alone.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the training owner where these scenarios appear in current lessons. Choose examples relevant to Finance, HR, reception or other teams. Check that the content was delivered through the awareness program, not just available in a course library.
requirement_guide.evidence: Lesson material can show the scenarios covered. Attendance, completion records or discussion results can show delivery. A phishing simulation may provide additional insight, but a simulation is not a mandatory IG1 artifact.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask the awareness owner: Do staff learn to question unusual payment or information requests? Are impersonation and physical-access tricks covered? How do we know the lesson reached the workforce, including roles handling sensitive requests?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for lessons limited to misspelled emails, no examples relevant to business roles, or licensed content never delivered. A successful simulated email test alone does not demonstrate the breadth of the training.

matrix.title: Train Workforce Members on Authentication Best Practices
matrix.authored_summary: Teach secure authentication and credential handling.
review_questions: Review authentication training and how it is delivered. CIS example topics include MFA, password composition and credential management.
Confirm practical instruction fits the authentication methods used by the workforce. A technical MFA configuration alone does not demonstrate training.
evidence_examples: Authentication lesson material with attendance or completion records.
Workforce guidance or knowledge checks used to reinforce the lesson.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach people how to authenticate safely—prove their identity when signing in. This includes useful instruction on passwords, handling credentials and multi-factor authentication, adapted to the methods the organization uses.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the training owner and IT to compare sign-in lessons with today's tools. Check whether staff learn what to do in realistic situations, such as an unexpected authentication prompt, rather than only learning terminology.
requirement_guide.evidence: Authentication lesson material and completion records can show what was taught and to whom. Job aids or knowledge checks may support understanding. A technical multi-factor configuration proves a different point from workforce training.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask the awareness owner: Do the lessons explain safe password and credential handling? Do staff know how to use our additional sign-in factors? Are instructions updated when the authentication method changes?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate training that names multi-factor authentication without explaining user behavior, outdated screenshots that confuse staff, or technical configuration offered as the only evidence that training occurred.

matrix.title: Train Workforce on Data Handling Best Practices
matrix.authored_summary: Teach safe storage, sharing and disposal of sensitive information.
review_questions: Review training on identifying sensitive data and securely storing, transferring, archiving and destroying it.
Confirm clear-screen and clear-desk practices are taught, including locking unattended screens, clearing physical/virtual whiteboards and securing data/assets.
evidence_examples: Data-handling and clear-screen/desk lesson material.
Training delivery records or exercises relevant to the organization's data handling.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach people to recognize sensitive information and handle it safely when storing, sharing, archiving and destroying it. Include practical clear-desk and clear-screen habits, such as locking an unattended screen and clearing sensitive whiteboards.
requirement_guide.start: Ask data owners and the training owner for lessons covering the information staff actually use. Trace a familiar record, such as a personnel file, through sharing, storage and disposal. Check physical and virtual workspace examples too.
requirement_guide.evidence: Data-handling and clear-desk/screen lesson materials can show topic coverage. Attendance records or relevant exercises can show delivery. A data-handling policy supplies context but does not establish that people were taught how to apply it.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask HR, data owners or the awareness owner: Can staff recognize sensitive records? Are secure transfer, archiving and destruction explained? Do lessons cover unattended screens, paper records and physical or virtual whiteboards?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for training covering email but not disposal, no examples of sensitive business data, or clear-desk advice that overlooks virtual whiteboards. Written rules alone may not demonstrate practical workforce instruction.

matrix.title: Train Workforce Members on Causes of Unintentional Data Exposure
matrix.authored_summary: Explain accidental disclosure and prevention.
review_questions: Review training on accidental exposure, such as sending data to the wrong recipient, losing portable devices or sharing with unintended audiences.
Confirm relevant examples and delivery records show the topic is taught, rather than covered only by a data-handling policy.
evidence_examples: Lessons or communications explaining accidental-exposure scenarios.
Attendance, completion or scenario-discussion records.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach people how information can be exposed accidentally, even without an attacker. Sending to the wrong person, sharing a link too broadly or losing a device are everyday examples staff should be able to recognize and avoid.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the training owner for accidental-disclosure examples relevant to daily work. Review how staff send, share and carry information. Check that lessons cover those situations and have actually reached the workforce.
requirement_guide.evidence: Lessons or communications can illustrate common mistakes. Completion, attendance or scenario-discussion records can show delivery. Real incident details are not necessary; safe examples can teach the same behavior without exposing sensitive information.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask the awareness owner: Do lessons explain wrong-recipient messages and overly broad sharing? Are lost devices and portable data covered? How do staff check the intended audience before sending or granting access?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate training focused entirely on malicious attacks, advice that ignores shared-link permissions, or policies with no practical examples. A lack of reported accidents does not demonstrate that people received this training.

matrix.title: Train Workforce Members on Recognizing and Reporting Security Incidents
matrix.authored_summary: Teach workers to identify and report potential incidents.
review_questions: Review training on recognizing a possible security incident and reporting it through the organization's reporting process.
Confirm workforce-facing instructions identify a usable reporting route. Compare training with current contacts so staff are not directed to obsolete channels.
evidence_examples: Incident-recognition/reporting training and completion records.
Current reporting instructions or exercise/discussion results where used.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach people to recognize a possible security incident and report it through the organization's process. They do not need to prove an attack occurred before knowing where to ask for help or raise a concern.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the awareness owner to show the recognition and reporting lesson. Compare its contacts and reporting route with current instructions. Check that examples make sense for ordinary staff, such as a lost device or suspicious message.
requirement_guide.evidence: Lesson material can explain warning signs and the reporting route. Completion records show delivery. A practice discussion or exercise may support understanding, but the training should agree with the actual reporting process.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask the training and incident owners: What signs are staff taught to recognize? Where should they report concerns? Are the training contacts current? Can a nontechnical employee understand what to do without first investigating the incident?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for obsolete phone numbers, instructions telling staff only to contact 'security' without a usable route, or lessons on recognition with nothing about reporting. A documented response plan alone does not establish workforce training.

matrix.title: Train Workforce on How to Identify and Report if Their Enterprise Assets are Missing Security Updates
matrix.authored_summary: Teach recognition and reporting of failed security updates.
review_questions: Review training showing the workforce how to identify and report outdated software patches or failures in automated processes and tools.
Confirm the instruction includes notifying IT about failures. An automated patch report alone does not show that this workforce topic was taught.
evidence_examples: Lessons or job aids explaining update/failure indicators and how to notify IT.
Training records or practical demonstrations used by the organization.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach people to notice outdated software patches and failures in automated tools, and report them to IT. Staff are not being asked to become patch administrators; they need to recognize warning signs and know how to get help.
requirement_guide.start: Ask IT what update or tool-failure messages users commonly see. Compare those with the awareness material and reporting instructions. Check that the examples explain both missing updates and failed automatic processes.
requirement_guide.evidence: Lessons, job aids or demonstrations can show the warning signs taught. Training records can show delivery. A patch deployment report supports technical operation but does not show that users were taught how to report a problem.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask the awareness owner and IT: Which update warnings should users report? How should they contact IT? Does training cover automation failures as well as missing patches? Are users told what to do without making unauthorized changes?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate advice to ignore repeated update errors, training covering only restart reminders, or no reporting route for failed tools. Technical automation does not remove the need for the workforce topic.

matrix.title: Train Workforce on the Dangers of Connecting to and Transmitting Enterprise Data Over Insecure Networks
matrix.authored_summary: Cover insecure connections and safe remote/home networking.
review_questions: Review training on the risks of connecting to insecure networks and transmitting enterprise data over them.
Where remote workers exist, confirm training includes secure configuration of home network infrastructure. Check that delivery reaches the relevant workforce.
evidence_examples: Insecure-network and, where relevant, home-network training material.
Attendance/completion records or remote-worker guidance supporting delivery.

requirement_guide.plain: Teach people the risks of connecting to insecure networks and sending work information across them. Where remote workers exist, include secure setup of home network equipment. This is workforce guidance, not a requirement for employees to become network engineers.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the training owner how lessons address work away from the office. For remote staff, review the practical home-network guidance. Compare examples with the network situations the workforce actually encounters.
requirement_guide.evidence: Lessons on insecure connections and relevant home-network guidance can show coverage. Completion or attendance records can show delivery to the workforce. A remote-access product alone does not demonstrate that these topics were taught.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask HR or the awareness owner: Do staff understand risks on public or otherwise insecure networks? Do remote workers receive usable home-network setup guidance? Where can they ask for help when unsure about a connection?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for training limited to office Wi-Fi, home-network guidance omitted for remote workers, or technical instructions too unclear to use. Avoid assuming that a protected work device makes every network situation safe.

matrix.title: Establish and Maintain an Inventory of Service Providers
matrix.authored_summary: Inventory providers, classifications and accountable contacts.
review_questions: Compare the provider inventory with known services and relationships. Confirm it includes all known providers, their classifications and an internal enterprise contact for each.
Verify annual review/update and updates after significant changes. Do not turn this inventory safeguard into a mandatory provider-assessment program (standalone safeguard 15.5 is IG3).
evidence_examples: Provider inventory with classifications and designated contacts.
Annual reconciliation or change records compared with contracts, purchasing or service records.

requirement_guide.plain: Know which service providers the organization uses, how they are classified and who inside the organization is responsible for the relationship. Review the inventory annually and after significant changes. This inventory safeguard is not a separate mandate to audit every supplier.
requirement_guide.start: Ask procurement, Finance and department leads for their provider lists. Reconcile them with contracts and service records. Add missing classifications and internal contacts, including services purchased directly by a department.
requirement_guide.evidence: A provider register can show names, classifications and internal contacts. Purchasing or contract records can help check completeness. Dated annual reconciliation and change records can show the inventory stays current.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask procurement and business owners: Which providers support your work? Are they in the shared inventory? What classification and internal contact does each have? How are new or ended relationships reflected in the list?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate recurring service payments with no inventory entry, provider contacts confused with internal relationship owners, or classifications left blank. A contracts folder may not be a maintained inventory with the required details.

matrix.title: Designate Personnel to Manage Incident Handling
matrix.authored_summary: Identify incident leadership, backup coverage and internal oversight.
review_questions: Confirm a lead and at least one backup are designated to manage incident handling, coordinating and documenting response and recovery.
If providers perform incident handling, confirm at least one internal person oversees their work. Verify designations are reviewed annually and after significant relevant changes.
evidence_examples: Incident-handling role assignments, including lead, backup and any internal provider overseer.
Dated reviews, responsibility records or provider agreements supporting the assignments.

requirement_guide.plain: Name a lead and at least one backup to coordinate and document incident response and recovery. If a provider handles incidents, keep at least one internal person overseeing that work. Review the assignments annually and after significant relevant changes.
requirement_guide.start: Ask management who would coordinate a security incident today and who would cover their absence. Check those assignments against the documented responsibilities. If response is outsourced, identify the internal overseer as well as the provider contact.
requirement_guide.evidence: Role assignments or an incident plan can show the lead, backup and coordination duties. Provider agreements may clarify external responsibilities. Dated reviews and personnel-change updates can establish that the assignments are current.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask management: Who leads and documents response and recovery? Who is the backup? If our provider acts, who internally oversees it? Have personnel or service changes affected these assignments since the last annual review?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for a single named person with no backup, a departed employee still listed, or outsourcing with no internal oversight. A provider's response capability does not automatically establish the organization's own responsibilities.

matrix.title: Establish and Maintain Contact Information for Reporting Security Incidents
matrix.authored_summary: Verify incident notification contacts.
review_questions: Review contact information for parties that need incident notification. Consider the organization's actual stakeholders, including providers, insurers or authorities where relevant.
Confirm contact details are verified annually. This notification list is distinct from the workforce's reporting instructions in 17.3; not every example stakeholder must apply to every organization.
evidence_examples: Incident-notification contact list relevant to the organization.
Dated annual contact verification or provider confirmation records.

requirement_guide.plain: Keep current contact details for parties who may need notification about an incident, and verify them annually. The relevant parties depend on the organization; examples such as providers, insurers or authorities are not a universal list for every incident.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the incident owner which internal and external parties belong on the notification list. Check that usable contact details exist for those parties. Review the latest annual verification rather than assuming an old directory remains valid.
requirement_guide.evidence: An incident-notification list can identify relevant recipients and routes. Dated checks or contact confirmations can establish currency. Contract or insurance contact information may help corroborate entries without defining new notification obligations.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask the incident owner: Who may need notification under our arrangements? How would we reach them? When were the details last verified? Is this list distinct from the instructions employees use to report a concern?
requirement_guide.gaps: Investigate obsolete numbers, missing contacts for important providers, or a generic stakeholder list never checked for relevance. Listing an authority does not by itself establish when a legal notification obligation applies.

matrix.title: Establish and Maintain an Enterprise Process for Reporting Incidents
matrix.authored_summary: Document and communicate the workforce incident-reporting process.
review_questions: Review the documented workforce incident-reporting process for reporting timeframes, recipients, reporting mechanism and minimum information to provide.

Confirm all workforce members can access it. Verify annual review and review after significant changes affecting the process; workforce availability does not mean publishing internal details to the internet.
evidence_examples: Reporting instructions showing all four required elements.
Workforce access/communication records and dated annual or change-driven reviews.

requirement_guide.plain: Give the whole workforce accessible instructions for reporting incidents: when to report, to whom, by what method and what minimum information to provide. Review the instructions annually and after significant relevant changes. Accessible to staff does not mean publicly posting internal details.
requirement_guide.start: Ask the incident owner for the workforce reporting instructions. Check the four required elements and try finding the instructions as an ordinary staff member. Compare contacts and channels with the current reporting arrangements.
requirement_guide.evidence: A staff procedure, intranet page or job aid can state the reporting steps. Communication or access records can support workforce availability. Dated reviews and revisions show that changes to contacts or reporting methods are reflected.
requirement_guide.ask: Ask the incident and HR owners: How quickly should staff report under our process? Who receives reports, through which channel, and what information is needed? Can every workforce group find the instructions? When were they last reviewed?
requirement_guide.gaps: Look for instructions saying only 'report promptly' without the organization's timeframes, missing recipients or minimum details, or a page some staff cannot access. A response plan restricted to the incident team may not serve workforce reporting.

Collect observations and resolve inventory differences. Check actual execution rather than a policy statement alone.

matrix.title: Use a Passive Asset Discovery Tool
matrix.control_name: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
matrix.authored_summary: Discover connected assets passively; use the results to refresh the asset inventory at least weekly.
matrix.source_timing_explanation: At least weekly: review discovery results and use them to update inventory. Passive discovery operates between those reviews.
review_questions: [Requirement check 1.5] Were passive-discovery results reviewed and used to update inventory at least weekly? [Explanatory prompt] Which networks or weeks lack supporting records?

Confirm monitored network segments and reconcile dated discoveries to inventory entries. Trace an unknown asset through ownership and authorization decisions; check gaps between weekly reconciliations.

Scope and timing: At least weekly: review discovery results and use them to update inventory. Passive discovery operates between those reviews. Use dated operational records; completing this governance Review does not itself demonstrate technical execution.
evidence_examples: Sensor coverage map, discovery output, dated inventory change log or provider reconciliation record.
Relevant existing records or equivalent support may be linked; these examples are not mandatory files.

requirement_guide.plain: Discover connected assets passively; use the results to refresh the asset inventory at least weekly. A sensor reports what it sees; someone or an operating process must use that information to keep the inventory current. Ask the network operator for one recent discovery and its inventory disposition.
requirement_guide.start: Confirm monitored network segments and reconcile dated discoveries to inventory entries. Trace an unknown asset through ownership and authorization decisions; check gaps between weekly reconciliations. Start with the responsible team or provider and existing operational records; do not invent assignments or completed activity.
requirement_guide.evidence: Sensor coverage map, discovery output, dated inventory change log or provider reconciliation record. Use representative existing support and explain scope, dates and limitations.

requirement_guide.gaps: Unmonitored segments; recurring discoveries never added to inventory; weekly reconciliation missed. Use existing Findings and Actions for follow-up. Event-driven work is not automatically detected by Omnisciente.

evidence_examples: Approved script list, enforcement configuration, safe allow/block test results, reassessment record.
Relevant existing records or equivalent support may be linked; these examples are not mandatory files.

requirement_guide.plain: Enforce execution of authorized scripts only and block others; reassess at least every six months. An approved list alone does not stop execution. Digital signatures and version control are examples, not a mandate to buy a specific tool or use both in every environment.

Relevant existing records or equivalent support may be linked; these examples are not mandatory files.
